meaning: The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa

phonemes.desc: Alveolar trill [r] with long open ā [aː]; the length on the first syllable is the very mark plain ASCII deletes.
Voiced labial approximant [ʋ] — softer than English v — plus short a [ɐ].
Retroflex nasal [ɳ], the tongue curled back toward the palate; the final a is short [ɐ].

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAA-vuh-nuh' — long open first syllable, a soft w-like v, and a tongue-curled n for the ṇ.

kin.label: Sanskrit root
kin.form: √ru 'to roar, cry out' — rāvaṇa is 'the Roarer'; the epic explains the name at the shaking of Kailāsa (Monier-Williams s.v.; Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇḍa 16).

kin.label: Prakrit
kin.form: Rayaṇa — the form of the name in Vimalasūri's Paümacariya, the Jain Rāmāyaṇa in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit.

kin.label: Tamil
kin.form: Iṟāvaṇaṉ — the Tamil form, with prothetic i-, of the Cilappatikāram and the later Kamba Rāmāyaṇam tradition.

pronunciation.note: Rāvaṇa is Tier 1 because the Sanskrit form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: long ā and retroflex ṇ, both gone from plain ravana.

domains.title: Ten-Headed King
domains.subtitle: Ten-Headed King, Lanka
domains.lead: Rāvaṇa is the ten-headed king of Laṅkā in the Sanskrit Rāmāyaṇa — grandson of a mind-born sage, son of a demon princess, devotee of Śiva, master of the Vedas, and the abductor whose war against Rāma costs him his kingdom, his sons, and his life. The epic builds him as its most learned villain: every virtue but one.

cards.name: Ten-Headed King
cards.desc: Daśagrīva — ten heads, twenty arms; later readers counted the four Vedas and six śāstras among the ten.

cards.name: King of Laṅkā
cards.desc: Son of the sage Viśravas and the daitya princess Kaikasi; sovereign of the golden island fortress and its rākṣasa hosts (Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇḍa 9).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Rāvaṇa recovers the long ā and retroflex ṇ that plain ASCII ravana flattens.

cards.name: Epic Attestation
cards.desc: Chief antagonist of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa — and, in the Jain Paümacariya, the noblest king of the story.

symbols.name: Ten heads (daśānana)
symbols.meaning: The multiplied mind; later tradition glosses the ten as the four Vedas and six śāstras — mastery worn as anatomy.

symbols.name: The Pushpaka vimāna
symbols.meaning: His sky-going chariot, won from his brother Kubera — the vehicle of the abduction and, at the epic's end, of Rāma's triumphal return.

symbols.name: The Śivatāṇḍava stotra
symbols.meaning: The hymn he sang with crushed arms beneath Kailāsa — the one language, devotion, that he never lost.

symbols.name: Brahmā's boon
symbols.meaning: Near-invulnerability to gods, gandharvas, and demons — and the fatal contempt that left men out of the list.

symbols.name: The golden city of Laṅkā
symbols.meaning: The island fortress his brother Kubera ruled before him, built of gold by the divine architect Viśvakarman.

mythology.lead: The Rāmāyaṇa builds Rāvaṇa as a complete king — scholar, musician, ascetic, conqueror of the three worlds — whose single failure of self-command draws Rāma across the ocean. His story spans the epic's frame: born in its seventh book, he dies in its sixth.

myths.title: Born of Sage and Demoness
myths.text: In the Rāmāyaṇa's seventh book the villain's pedigree is nobler than his deeds: his father is Viśravas, a sage of flawless conduct, son of Pulastya, whom Brahmā generated from his own mind; his mother is Kaikasi, daughter of the daitya king Sumāli. From their union came four children — Rāvaṇa, the massive Kumbhakarṇa, the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, and the fierce Śūrpaṇakhā (Vālmīki, Uttarakāṇḍa 9–11). The young Daśagrīva performed a tapas of terrifying austerity — standing amid five fires, his arms raised, for a thousand years — until Brahmā, unable to refuse him, granted near-invulnerability: no god, gandharva, yakṣa, or demon might kill him. Men he omitted from the request, in contempt for their weakness (Uttarakāṇḍa 10). Later tellings deepen the bargain — nine times he offered his own head into the fire, and nine times it grew back, until ten heads stood where one had been. The epic's point is exact: its monster is born of a sage's house, and his doom is written into his own wish.

myths.title: The Shaking of Kailāsa
myths.text: Striding forth to conquer the quarters, Rāvaṇa found the way to Śiva barred by the bull-bannered gatekeeper Nandin; mocked for his boast, he took hold of the mountain itself and began to wrench it from its roots, so that the peaks, forests, and every creature upon them cried out (Vālmīki, Uttarakāṇḍa 16). Śiva pressed the peak down with the toe of his foot and pinned the upstart's arms beneath it; the agony tore a roar from him so tremendous that the three worlds shook, and the pleased god named him on the spot: Rāvaṇa, 'he who roars' — for older tradition the roar was the cry of the crushed, and Kālidāsa would later retell the whole confrontation in the Kumārasambhava (canto 7). Crushed but unrepentant, Rāvaṇa sang — the Śivatāṇḍava stotra, the hymn still recited in Śaiva mornings — until the mountain lifted and Śiva, mollified, gave him the sword Candrahāsa. The myth defines him in a single tableau: strength enough to move a mountain, devotion enough to sing to the god who crushes him, and a roar that becomes his name.

myths.title: The Golden Deer
myths.text: In the forest of Pañcavaṭī the king of Laṅkā played the long game of vengeance. His sister Śūrpaṇakhā came home mutilated by Lakṣmaṇa after her advances; his cousins Khara and Dūṣaṇa marched out of Janasthāna with fourteen thousand troops and were annihilated. Then came the abduction itself: Mārīca, master of illusion, took the shape of a golden deer with silver spots, and Rāma, beguiled, chased it deep into the wood; the dying demon mimicked Rāma's voice crying for help, and Sītā — against her own knowledge of the rules of the forest — sent Lakṣmaṇa after him. With the hermitage empty, Rāvaṇa approached in the guise of a wandering ascetic and carried Sītā off through the sky in the Pushpaka chariot. The aged vulture Jaṭāyu, her only defender, struck until his wings were shorn and fell dying; from his last words Rāma learned the abductor's name. Every element of that hour is answered in kind before the epic ends — the epic's economy of violence is exact, and the abduction buys the destruction of everything Rāvaṇa loves.

myths.title: The Siege of Laṅkā
myths.text: Rāma's army was monkeys and bears under Sugrīva and Hanumān, and the ocean itself was crossed at Rāma's word: the Nala Setu, a bridge of mountain-peaks dropped into the sea from Rāmeśvaram to Laṅkā (Yuddhakāṇḍa 22). The siege that followed is the epic's great battle-book. Meghnāda, Rāvaṇa's sorcerer-son called Indrajit, bound the whole monkey host with the serpent-noose of the nāgāstra, and later struck Lakṣmaṇa down with the Brahmāstra itself; only the Himalayan herb Suṣeṇa prescribed, flown in by Hanumān, called him back from death. Vibhīṣaṇa — Rāvaṇa's own brother — had urged the return of Sītā and, his counsel scorned, crossed to Rāma's camp; from him the allies learned the secret of Indrajit's sacrificial rites and killed him at his own ritual. Kumbhakarṇa woke from his six-month sleep and fell like a landslide. The epic's verdict is spoken in its council scenes: Laṅkā does not fall to monkeys, but to a king who will listen to no one.

myths.title: The Death of the Ten-Headed King
myths.text: The last duel ran a day and a night. Rāma cut away head after head — and the necks sprouted anew, the severed heads regenerating like serpents' tails — until Vibhīṣaṇa revealed where the boon had hidden his brother's life, and Rāma strung the great arrow that Agastya had given him, charged with the power of the wind-god, and loosed it through the chest (Yuddhakāṇḍa 108–111). The ten-headed king fell as Vṛtra fell to Indra's bolt, and the earth shook to its oceans. What follows is the epic's most revealing grace-note: Rāma commands the full funeral rites for his enemy and says that no greater hero had ever lived, and the dying king, through Vibhīṣaṇa, gives Sītā his blessing and pronounces her chaste before the whole world. In the frame of the Uttarakāṇḍa and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (7.1), Rāvaṇa had never truly been a demon at all, but Jaya — Viṣṇu's own gatekeeper, cursed to three enemy-births as the price of a wish. The epic dispatches its enemies; it never once permits itself to despise them.

lore.syncretism: The Jains refused the epic's verdict. In Vimalasūri's Prakrit Paümacariya (c. 3rd–5th century CE), the villain of Vālmīki becomes the noble King Rayaṇa of Laṅgka, a Jain layman of scrupulous conduct — it is Lakṣmaṇa who is the ruthless one, and the virtuous Rayaṇa who attains heaven. Southeast Asia recast him again: in the Thai Ramakien he is Thotsakan, the ten-faced titan of Ayutthaya drama, still the arch-villain but magnificent; in Cambodia's Reamker he is Krong Reap, the giant king of Laṅkā. In parts of South Asia the demon became a deity: villages in Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh keep Rāvaṇa shrines, and the Gonds of Bastar claim descent from a 'Rāvaṇa king' of old. His Śaiva devotion also survived independently of his epic crimes — the Śivatāṇḍava is still recited at Śiva's morning worship, and Ayurvedic tradition names him among its legendary physician-authors. The traditions disagree on whether he is to be burned or bowed to; both have been done, in different places, for two thousand years.
lore.culturalLegacy: Every autumn at Dussehra, across India and the diaspora, towering effigies of Rāvaṇa — ten-headed, twenty-armed, stuffed with firecrackers — are burned to cheers, reenacting the epic's climax on the festival that celebrates Rāma's victory. The ritual has its dissenters: in Bisrakh, the village near Delhi that claims his birthplace, some families keep mourning on the burning-day, and in Bastar, Gond tradition counts him an ancestor to be honored. His name lives in music through the rāvaṇahatthā, the spike-fiddle of Rajasthani folk players long described as his invention and famous in the West since the 1960s as the ravanastron, a claimed ancestor of the violin family. Modern retellings — from Bhavabhūti's sympathetic eighth-century Uttararāmacarita to television's 1987 Rāmāyaṇ and twenty-first-century novels narrated from Laṅkā's side — keep returning to him: the villain whose learning, grief, and grandeur make the hero's victory cost something.
lore.extendedMeditation: Rāvaṇa is the epic's portrait of a mind that knows everything except how to yield. Ten heads — later glossed as the four Vedas and the six śāstras — and twenty arms; a singer whose hymn still opens Śaiva mornings; a conqueror who rode the Pushpaka to the ends of the three worlds; a king whose council scenes are a seminar on statecraft that he consistently fails to heed. The Rāmāyaṇa's deepest teaching is spoken by his own brother: give Sītā back, and live. He cannot, and the epic spends six books showing precisely what it costs a civilization when its most capable man cannot take advice. In this he is disturbingly modern — the expert, the genius, the tenfold mind that has read everything and changed nothing in itself. Restoring his name matters the way the epic's balance does: Rāvaṇa, with its long ā and curled ṇ, stands for a tradition that made even its demons learned and refused to write any man off as merely evil.

lore.archaeology: There is no material record of Rāvaṇa — no inscription, coin, or image survives from any period that names him, and the giant belongs entirely to the textual tradition, whose oldest witnesses are the medieval manuscripts of the Rāmāyaṇa itself. The landscape, however, has been thoroughly claimed by the epic. In Sri Lanka — Laṅkā of the tradition — the rock fortress of Sigīrya is popularly his palace (in fact the work of King Kāśyapa I, fifth century CE), and the cave above the falls at Ella is toured as Rāvaṇa's own. Between India and the island runs Ādām's Bridge, the chain of shoals the epic calls Nala's bridge (Yuddhakāṇḍa 22), and at Rāmeśvaram in Tamil Nadu the Rāmanāthaswāmy temple stands at the epic's launching point, its corridors among the longest in India. The archaeology of Rāvaṇa is thus the archaeology of reception — geology, temples, and place-names retelling the story in stone.
